lesson.title: Arithmetic Sequences: Counting by a Fixed Step
lesson.summary: Introduces arithmetic sequences as ordered lists of numbers that grow or shrink by the same fixed amount each step, and shows how to predict any term without listing them all.
lesson.body:
You already know that numbers can be arranged in order and compared, added, or subtracted. An arithmetic sequence takes that idea and turns it into a pattern: it's an ordered list of numbers, called terms, where you get from one term to the next by adding the same fixed amount every single time. That fixed amount is called the common difference, and it's what gives the sequence its rhythm ,  once you know the starting number and the common difference, the entire list is determined forever, no guessing required.

Think about the sequence 2, 5, 8, 11, 14. To go from 2 to 5 you add 3. From 5 to 8, you add 3 again. From 8 to 11, still 3. That repeated, unchanging step is the whole mechanism behind an arithmetic sequence ,  it isn't multiplying, doubling, or doing anything fancy; it's just steady, constant addition. Because the step never changes, the sequence grows at a perfectly even rate, which is why arithmetic sequences feel so predictable compared to a random list of numbers.

That predictability lets you skip ahead without writing out every term. Since each new term is the previous term plus the common difference, the second term is the first term plus one step, the third term is the first term plus two steps, and so on. In general, if the first term is called a₁ and the common difference is d, then the nth term is a_n = a₁ + (n − 1)d. The "n − 1" matters because the first term itself hasn't had any step added to it yet ,  it's the starting point, not a result of adding d.

Try it on the sequence above: a₁ = 2 and d = 3. To find the 5th term without listing all five numbers, compute a₅ = 2 + (5 − 1)(3) = 2 + 12 = 14. That matches what you'd get by counting up by 3s four times, which is exactly the point ,  the formula just compresses the repeated addition into one calculation.

The common difference doesn't have to be positive. Consider 20, 15, 10, 5: here each term is the previous one minus 5, so d = −5. Using the formula, the 4th term is a₄ = 20 + (4 − 1)(−5) = 20 − 15 = 5, which checks out. A negative common difference simply means the sequence steadily decreases instead of increasing, but the underlying mechanism ,  adding the same fixed amount every time ,  is unchanged.

What makes arithmetic sequences worth studying is this uniform rate of change: every step forward changes the value by exactly the same amount, never more, never less. That steady behavior is the seed of ideas you'll meet later involving constant rates of change, so getting comfortable now with spotting the common difference and using it to jump straight to any term will pay off well beyond this single topic.
